recipe: Remember that each call to a custom hook is completely independent — it shares stateful logic but not the state itself. If you need to share actual state between multiple components, lift it up and pass it down instead.
trigger_condition: You are considering whether to share state between components via a custom hook or via props.
evidence: Custom Hooks let you share *stateful logic* but not *state itself.* Each call to a Hook is completely independent from every other call to the same Hook.

recipe: Pass reactive values (props or state) into your custom hook as arguments; the hook will always receive the latest values because it re-renders together with the component.
trigger_condition: Your custom hook needs to react to changing props or state from the calling component.
evidence: Because custom Hooks re-render together with your component, they always receive the latest props and state.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Extract effect code into a custom hook to simplify your component, passing the relevant reactive values as arguments so the effect still responds to changes.

recipe: Don't extract a custom Hook for every small piece of duplicated code; some duplication is acceptable and over-extraction adds unnecessary indirection.
trigger_condition: When deciding whether to extract a minor piece of duplicated logic into a custom Hook.
evidence: You don't need to extract a custom Hook for every little duplicated bit of code. Some duplication is fine.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Whenever you write an Effect, evaluate whether wrapping it in a custom Hook would make the intent and data flow clearer.
trigger_condition: When writing a useEffect in a component that synchronizes with an external system.
evidence: whenever you write an Effect, consider whether it would be clearer to also wrap it in a custom Hook
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Keep separate Effects separate when they synchronize different things; extract only the shared logic into a common Hook rather than merging unrelated Effects into one.
trigger_condition: When multiple Effects in a component share similar code patterns but serve different purposes.
evidence: They synchronize two different things, so you shouldn't merge them into one Effect.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Start by choosing your custom Hook's name before extracting; if you can't pick a clear name, the logic is too coupled to the component and isn't ready to be extracted yet.
trigger_condition: When deciding whether a block of logic is a good candidate for extraction into a custom Hook.
evidence: Start by choosing your custom Hook's name. If you struggle to pick a clear name, it might mean that your Effect is too coupled to the rest of your component's logic, and is not yet ready to be extracted.

recipe: Name custom Hooks so clearly that even a non-developer can guess what the Hook does, what it accepts, and what it returns.
trigger_condition: When naming a new custom Hook.
evidence: Ideally, your custom Hook's name should be clear enough that even a person who doesn't write code often could have a good guess about what your custom Hook does, what it takes, and what it returns
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: When writing a custom Hook that wraps useEffect, remember the linter only checks direct useEffect calls, so you must manually verify that your Hook's dependencies are complete and correct.
trigger_condition: You are creating a custom Hook that internally calls useEffect and passes in a function or other value that could change between renders.
evidence: the linter won't warn you about it because the linter only checks direct `useEffect` calls. It won't know about your Hook.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: When writing an Effect, start by using the React API directly with raw useEffect calls before extracting any custom Hook.
trigger_condition: You need to add side-effect logic to a component and are deciding whether to write it inline or wrap it in a custom Hook.

recipe: Design your custom Hook's API to constrain what the calling code can do, making the component more declarative rather than providing a very abstract general-purpose utility.
trigger_condition: You are finalizing the public API of a custom Hook and are deciding how much flexibility to expose to the caller.
evidence: A good custom Hook makes the calling code more declarative by constraining what it does.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Wrap your Effects in custom Hooks so that when React introduces a better built-in API, you can swap the implementation without touching any component code.
trigger_condition: You are implementing a side effect (e.g., syncing with an external system) and anticipate that a more specific React API may replace your current approach.
evidence: Wrapping your Effects in custom Hooks makes it easier to upgrade your code when these solutions become available.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Extract common idioms from your app's components into custom Hooks to keep component code focused on intent and reduce the frequency of writing raw Effects.
trigger_condition: You notice the same side-effect pattern repeated across multiple components in your application.
evidence: you might find it helpful to start extracting common idioms from your app's components into custom Hooks. This will keep your components' code focused on the intent, and let you avoid writing raw Effects very often.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: If you need data fetching, wrap it in a custom Hook like useData so that migrating to a future built-in data fetching API requires fewer changes than rewriting raw Effects in every component.
trigger_condition: You are implementing data fetching in your React app and want to future-proof the code against upcoming React APIs.
evidence: If you use custom Hooks like `useData` above in your app, it will require fewer changes to migrate to the eventually recommended approach than if you write raw Effects in every component manually.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Extract shared setup logic (like animation loops) from one custom hook into a dedicated hook to avoid duplication across multiple hooks.
trigger_condition: You find yourself duplicating the same setup logic (e.g., animation loop) across multiple custom hooks.
evidence: you could extract the logic for setting up the animation loop out of `useFadeIn` into a custom `useAnimationLoop` Hook
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: When multiple Effects need to coordinate (e.g., chaining animations), extract the imperative logic out of Effects and Hooks entirely into a separate module or class.
trigger_condition: You need to chain or coordinate multiple Effects together, such as for multiple animations.
evidence: The more coordination between Effects is needed (for example, to chain multiple animations), the more it makes sense to extract that logic out of Effects and Hooks
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Once you extract imperative logic into an external system, keep your Effects minimal so they only send messages to that system rather than containing the logic themselves.
trigger_condition: You have moved imperative logic (e.g., animation) outside of React into a class or module.
evidence: This lets your Effects stay simple because they only need to send messages to the system you've moved outside React.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Prefer implementing animations with plain CSS (keyframes) over JavaScript when the animation can be achieved with CSS, as it is simpler and more efficient.

source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Name custom hooks with the `use` prefix followed by a capital letter.
trigger_condition: You are creating a new custom hook.
evidence: Custom Hooks must be named starting with `use` followed by a capital letter.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Keep custom hooks purpose-specific rather than creating overly generic ones like `useMount`.
trigger_condition: You are designing the scope and naming of a new custom hook.
evidence: Don't create custom Hooks like `useMount`. Keep their purpose specific.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Wrap event handlers passed as arguments to custom hooks into Effect Events to avoid stale closure issues.
trigger_condition: Your custom hook receives an event handler as a parameter and uses it inside an Effect.
evidence: Wrap event handlers received by custom Hooks into Effect Events.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: When you pass a new parameter to a hook that is used inside an Effect, add that parameter to the Effect's dependency array so the Effect re-runs when it changes.
trigger_condition: You pass a value (like a delay) into a custom hook and use it inside an Effect.
evidence: You'll need to add `delay` to your Effect's dependencies. This ensures that a change in `delay` will reset the interval.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Write custom hook code as pure functions, just like component code, to ensure predictable behavior on every re-render.
trigger_condition: You are writing or reviewing the body of a custom hook.
evidence: The code of your custom Hooks should be pure, like your component's code.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Extract stateful logic from a component into a custom hook so the component no longer needs to import React hooks directly.
trigger_condition: Your component contains both state and an Effect that could be encapsulated in a hook.
evidence: Notice that `App.js` doesn't need to import `useState` or `useEffect` anymore.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Split out the logic that sets up the interval into a separate Hook called `useInterval` that takes an `onTick` callback and a `delay` argument, so your original hook only handles its own state management.
trigger_condition: When a custom hook performs multiple distinct tasks (e.g., setting up an interval AND incrementing a state variable) and you want to make the interval logic reusable.
evidence: Split out the logic that sets up the interval into a separate Hook called `useInterval`. It should take two arguments: the `onTick` callback, and the `delay`.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Keep a newly extracted custom hook focused on a single concern; it should only handle its specific responsibility and nothing else.
trigger_condition: When extracting logic from an existing hook into a new custom hook, ensure the new hook does not take on additional responsibilities.
evidence: The logic inside `useInterval` should set up and clear the interval. It doesn't need to do anything else.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Wrap the tick callback passed to a custom hook in `useEffectEvent` so you can omit it from the `useEffect` dependency array, preventing the effect from re-synchronizing on every re-render.
trigger_condition: When a custom hook passes a callback into a `useEffect` dependency array and that callback is recreated on every render, causing the effect to re-run unnecessarily.
evidence: This will allow you to omit `onTick` from dependencies of your Effect. The Effect won't re-synchronize on every re-render of the component, so the page background color change interval won't get reset every second before it has a chance to fire.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks

recipe: Implement a delayed-value hook by storing the delayed value in state, running an Effect on value change, and using `setTimeout` inside that Effect to update the delayed value after the specified delay.
trigger_condition: When you need a custom hook that returns a value from N milliseconds ago to create staggered or lagging behavior.
evidence: You'll need to store the `delayedValue` as a state variable inside your custom Hook. When the `value` changes, you'll want to run an Effect. This Effect should update `delayedValue` after the `delay`. You might find it helpful to call `setTimeout`.
source_name: react.dev learn: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks
